column1: # THE LAYERING (CLAUDE.md, Design rules; project/Coupling.scala `Layers`, `sbt couplingReport`, scripts/coupling-report):
# every production package's layer, bottom (0) up. A package may depend only on its own layer or a lower one; the
# coupling ratchet (scripts/ci/coupling_ratchet.py) fails on any package edge into a higher layer, and on a package no
# row names -- a new top-level package takes its place here in the commit that adds it. Loosening the table -- an `allow`
# row added, a package given another layer -- lands only in a commit carrying `Coupling: <why>` (the ratchet checks it).
#   layer<TAB><n><TAB><package prefix><TAB><why it sits there>   the longest prefix naming a package decides
#   allow<TAB><from>-><to><TAB><why>                          an upward edge kept on purpose (keep this list short)
# Packages inside one layer may still reach each other (services.* is one layer, and still one package cycle: the next
# cut). To cut an upward edge: move the type to the layer its users sit on, or put a small trait in the lower package.

column4: generic utilities and the HTTP layer: text, digests, clocks, fetches; they know no film, venue or setting (they take values)
the domain data -- films, venues, cities, countries -- and the pure readings of it
typed configuration: values resolved from the environment, which name models (a Country)
the external services' clients, beside the services that use them
the application: scraping, identity, enrichment, the read model, metrics -- one layer, cycles inside it allowed
the web tier's HTTP endpoints, view models and filters, over the services
the composition roots (AppLoader, WorkerMain and their wirings): everything is wired here, nothing depends on them
command-line programs run beside the app (FilmwebDiff, RosterAudit): built from the whole stack like a composition root
